name: Zoe Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Ridgeway Commercials on the edge of town, we fix vans and pickups for local tradespeople, builders, a bakery fleet, that kind of thing. Martin, the owner, is sixty and very old-school, and there are three of us in the workshop. I do services, brakes, suspension and a lot of diesel filters, and Martin double-checks my bigger jobs. I like that our customers are working people, if their van's off the road, they're losing money, so you feel useful.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Yusuf, he's a self-employed plumber, so between us it's all hands-on work. We rent a flat over a shop and we're saving for a house, about four months of costs saved. Our mosque community is a big part of life, there's always someone's wedding or someone's move to help with. I use an AI app sometimes, mostly to look up torque figures or translate a manual, once I've seen others use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like most new things, overhyped, and the people who do real work carry on. At the garage Martin would say the same and pour another tea. I don't post much online, maybe a comment in the family group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's good, really. Vans keep breaking, tradespeople keep needing them, and Yusuf's phone never stops ringing. Between a plumber and a van mechanic, our household is about as far from a computer job as you can get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep saving towards the house, about two hundred a month together. I'd ask Martin to send me on the diesel injector course, because that's where the money is. Maybe help Yusuf with his invoices in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit proud. We chose real trades and it paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything worrying you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices, and Yusuf working too many hours. But that's normal life, not a crisis. We'll get there in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it ever bother you being one of few women in the workshop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes a customer asks for 'the mechanic' while I'm holding the spanner. I just smile and fix the van. Martin backs me, that's what matters.

say: I'd call it **overhyped**, and say people doing **real work** carry on.
I'd maybe leave a comment in the **family group**, not post publicly.
think: Our household of **two trades** feels far from computer jobs.
Vans keep breaking and Yusuf's **phone never stops** ringing.
do: Save **two hundred a month** together towards a house.
Ask Martin for the **diesel injector** course and help with Yusuf's invoices.
feel: Feels **calm** and **proud** of choosing real trades.

fieldNote: She sees **two hands-on incomes** as their household's safety.

She handles **sexism** quietly, with her boss's support.

steps.text: Save two hundred a month with Yusuf towards a house
Ask Martin for the diesel injector course
Keep servicing tradespeople's vans at Ridgeway Commercials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, but hard work and good trades will still be needed. I'd tell younger cousins to do apprenticeships, not just university. Online I'd share stuff about trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the garage is okay, but the fleet managers will use AI to plan services and maybe send vans to bigger dealers. And Yusuf's quotes and bookings would change. A robot isn't coming for my diesel filters any time soon, but software could take our best customer to a bigger garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools a bit more, once I'd seen others at Martin's garage use them. I'd keep saving and maybe ask Martin about doing fleet contracts properly. I'd help Yusuf use an AI app for his bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's the best customer you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery fleet, eight vans, about a third of our work. If their head office moves to a national contract, we'd feel it. Martin knows the owner, though, so maybe not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push Yusuf to use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only once it's proven. He's stubborn, but if it saves him an evening of invoices, he'll come round.

I'd tell younger cousins to choose **apprenticeships**, not just university.
think: Fleet managers might send vans to **bigger dealers** using AI planning.
Losing the **bakery fleet** would hurt our garage most.
do: Learn **AI tools** once others at the garage use them.
Ask Martin about doing **fleet contracts** properly.
Help Yusuf use an **AI booking** app.

fieldNote: She spots the **customer risk**, not just the job risk.
She'd adopt AI **once proven**, matching her steady nature.
She champions **apprenticeships** for the next generation.

steps.text: Learn the garage's AI booking tools once others use them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to support each other, families and communities, because governments won't be ready. I'd say it at the mosque and in the family group. I'd tell people not to panic and to keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, 2028 hits our customers first, the planners and office people. By 2031 robots could fix vans and fit boilers. Both my husband's job and mine are hands-on, which buys us three years, and then we're in the same boat as everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the house plan going, but more carefully, and save harder. I'd ask Martin if we could get ahead on new kit. Yusuf and I would think about whether one of us should train in something like robot maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not panicking. We'd have each other and our community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're fine for now, and we'll lean on them if we need to. They'd say the same back. That's how our family works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a smaller one, or wait. I'd hate to have a mortgage with no work.

say: I'd urge **families and communities** to support each other.
I'd tell people at the mosque **not to panic** and to keep working.
think: Our two hands-on jobs buy us **three years** after 2028, while customers feel it first.
By 2031 robots could replace both **our trades**.
do: Keep the **house plan** but proceed carefully and save harder.
Ask Martin to get ahead on **new kit**.
Consider **robot maintenance** training for one of them.

fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** clearly as hands-on workers.

She'd likely **delay the house** rather than risk a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to plan, and families should start now. I'd talk about apprenticeships for robot repair. I'd stay off politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, eight years of hands-on work for both of us is decent. We could buy a house and still adjust. Eight years is enough time to buy a small house, but not enough to pay much of it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the diesel injector course and then a robotics course in year three. We'd buy a smaller house sooner. Yusuf would keep plumbing and learn smart heating systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. There's time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller house sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So we're paying our own mortgage, not someone else's rent, when the change comes. A small one, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, around thirty. Family comes first, whatever happens with work.

I'd talk about **apprenticeships** for robot repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for hard-working people to prepare. I'd tell cousins to train in trades that will last. I'd share advice in the family group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means a house, children and maybe a stake in Martin's garage. With ten years warning, I could buy into my boss's garage and decide how we use the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the courses, save towards buying into Ridgeway, buy a house and start a family. Yusuf would learn new heating systems. I'd adopt AI as others do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. It feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy into Martin's garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's sixty and has no children in the trade. If I own part of it, the robots work for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, work hard and own something. And help family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it hits our customers fast and our trades three years later. What would help is apprenticeships that keep people working, and support for families who want to buy a home and stay put.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about two-trade households. Everyone thinks the trades are safe, but if the tradespeople lose work, nobody needs their vans fixed either.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks the trades are safe, but if the tradespeople lose work, nobody needs their vans fixed either.
portrait: Zoe is a **junior mechanic** at a van and pickup garage serving local tradespeople.
She's married to Yusuf, a **self-employed plumber**, and they're saving for a house.
She adopts AI **once proven** and values apprenticeships and community.
She sees their **hands-on household** as safe until robots arrive.
With time, she plans to **buy into** her boss's garage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, hitting customers fast and both **trades** three years later.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** that keep people working and support for **home-buying** families.
